subject: Architecture
title: The Great Pyramid: Precision in Stone
description: Learn The Great Pyramid: Precision in Stone in one minute.

hook.text: The Great Pyramid contains 2.3 million blocks and was the tallest structure for 3,800 years.

buildup.text: Each base side is 756 feet long. The difference between the longest and shortest is under 2 inches.

discovery.text: Workers used copper tools, wooden sledges, and ramps — no iron, no pulleys, no wheels.

twist.text: Recent discoveries show workers were paid laborers, not slaves — they even had medical care.

climax.text: A workforce of 20,000 built it in about 20 years using nothing but human organization.

punchline.text: No cranes. No computers. Just planning that still baffles us.

quiz.question: How long was the Great Pyramid the tallest structure on Earth?

details.summary: The Great Pyramid at Giza was built around 2560 BCE with 2.3 million stone blocks, each averaging 2.5 tons. Its base is level to within 2.1 centimeters across 230 meters.
details.whyItMatters: The Great Pyramid's precision reveals that ancient Egyptian engineering was far more sophisticated than commonly assumed. Achieving this accuracy with copper tools and no telescopes required deep understanding of astronomy, geometry.
takeaways: 2.3 million blocks averaging 2.5 tons each, built around 2560 BCE
Base level to within 2.1 cm across 230 meters
Aligned to true north with 3/60th of a degree accuracy

faq.question: How did they achieve such precise alignment?
faq.answer: Most likely by observing the rising and setting points of circumpolar stars and bisecting the angle between them to find true north. Water-filled trenches established level surfaces. Simple but carefully applied techniques achieved remarkable accuracy through patient, methodical work.

faq.question: How long did construction take?
faq.answer: Approximately 20 years under Pharaoh Khufu, requiring roughly 10-20 blocks placed per hour during working periods. A workforce of 20,000-30,000 organized in rotating crews managed quarrying, transport, and placement simultaneously across different sections of the pyramid.
